Learn more × License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2602.07374v1 [cs.CL] 07 Feb 2026 TernaryLM: Memory-Efficient Language Modeling via Native 1-Bit Quantization with Adaptive Layer-wise Scaling Nisharg Nargund Affiliation: KIIT Bhubaneshwar, India and Priyesh Shukla Affiliation: IIIT Hyderabad, India Abstract Large language models (LLMs) achieve remarkable performance but demand substantial computational resources, limiting deployment on edge devices and resource-constrained environments. We present TernaryLM, a 132M-parameter transformer architecture that employs native 1-bit ternary quantization { − 1 , 0 , + 1 } \{-1,0,+1\} during training, achieving significant memory reduction without sacrificing language modeling capability. Unlike post-training quantization approaches that quantize pre-trained full-precision models, TernaryLM learns quantization-aware representations from scratch using straight-through estimators and adaptive per-layer scaling factors. Our extensive experiments demonstrate: (1) validation perplexity of 58.42 on TinyStories, competitive with full-precision baselines; (2) strong downstream transfer with 82.47% F1 on MRPC paraphrase detection; (3) 2.4 × 	imes memory reduction (498MB vs 1.2GB) with comparable inference latency; and (4) stable training dynamics across diverse corpora. We provide comprehensive layer-wise quantization analysis revealing that middle transformer layers exhibit highest compatibility with extreme quantization, informing future non-uniform precision strategies. Our results challenge conventional assumptions about minimum precision requirements for language understanding and establish native 1-bit training as a viable paradigm for efficient neural language models. Our implementation and trained models are publicly available at https://github.com/1nisharg/TernaryLM-Memory-Efficient-Language-Modeling . Index Terms: neural network quantization, 1-bit neural networks, language models, efficient deep learning, ternary quantization, transformers. I Introduction The advent of large language models (LLMs) has revolutionized natural language processing, achieving unprecedented performance across tasks ranging from question answering to code generation [ 1 , 2 ] . However, these advances come at substantial computational cost: a 7-billion parameter model requires over 14GB of memory in half-precision (FP16) format, while inference latency can exceed 100ms per token on consumer hardware [ 3 ] . This computational barrier severely constrains practical deployment. Edge devices, mobile platforms, and embedded systems—where privacy-preserving on-device inference is increasingly important—cannot accommodate such resource demands. Even cloud deployment faces economic pressure as inference costs scale with model size and user demand. Quantization offers a principled solution by reducing numerical precision of model weights and activations. Post-training quantization (PTQ) methods successfully compress models to 8-bit [ 3 ] or 4-bit [ 4 , 5 ] representations with minimal quality degradation. However, pushing quantization below 4 bits typically causes severe performance collapse, particularly for autoregressive language modeling where error accumulates across generation steps. Key Research Question: Can language models be trained natively with 1-bit precision while preserving the representational capacity necessary for coherent language understanding? We address this question by introducing TernaryLM , a decoder-only transformer trained from scratch with ternary weights { − 1 , 0 , + 1 } \{-1,0,+1\} across all projection matrices. Unlike prior approaches that apply quantization as a compression technique post-training, TernaryLM learns quantization-aware representations during optimization, allowing the network to adapt its internal structure to the discrete weight constraint. Our contributions are: 1. Viable 1-bit language modeling: We demonstrate that native ternary quantization achieves validation perplexity of 58.42 on TinyStories, establishing that discrete { − 1 , 0 , + 1 } \{-1,0,+1\} weights can capture sufficient representational complexity for coherent language generation. 2. Downstream task transfer: Fine-tuning on MRPC yields 82.47% F1 score with only a 2.5% gap from BERT-Base, proving that quantized representations support effective gradient-based adaptation. 3. Practical efficiency gains: TernaryLM achieves 2.4 × 	imes memory reduction (498MB vs 1,197MB) while maintaining latency parity (9.41ms vs 9.52ms per token), enabling deployment on memory-constrained devices. 4. Comprehensive quantization analysis: Layer-wise sparsity profiling reveals that middle layers (L5-L9) exhibit highest quantization compatibility (60-62% sparsity scores), while early and late layers require more careful treatment—guiding future mixed-precision strategies. 5. Cross-corpus stability: Training dynamics remain stable across datasets with varying entropy characteristics (TinyStories and WritingPrompts), demonstrating robustness of our optimization protocol. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section II reviews related work on neural network quantization and efficient language models. Section III details the TernaryLM architecture and training protocol. Section IV presents experimental results including pre-training, fine-tuning, and efficiency analysis. Section V provides in-depth analysis of quantization dynamics. Section VI concludes with discussion and future directions. II Related Work II-A Post-Training Quantization Post-training quantization (PTQ) compresses pre-trained models by reducing weight and activation precision without retraining. Early work established 8-bit integer quantization as a practical compression technique with minimal accuracy loss [ 6 ] . For language models, LLM.int8() [ 3 ] introduced mixed-precision decomposition to handle outlier activations that otherwise degrade quantized model quality. Pushing to 4-bit precision, GPTQ [ 4 ] employs layer-wise optimal brain compression with second-order information, while AWQ [ 5 ] identifies activation-aware scaling factors that protect salient weights from quantization error. These methods achieve impressive compression ratios (4 × 	imes over FP16) while maintaining task performance on instruction-following benchmarks. However, PTQ approaches struggle below 4 bits. The fundamental limitation is that quantization is applied after the model has learned representations optimized for full-precision computation—forcing discrete approximation onto continuous learned weights introduces irreducible error that compounds during autoregressive generation. II-B Quantization-Aware Training Quantization-aware training (QAT) addresses PTQ limitations by incorporating quantization into the training process itself. The key challenge is gradient propagation through discrete operations. The straight-through estimator (STE) [ 7 ] approximates gradients by treating the quantization function as identity during backpropagation, enabling optimization despite non-differentiable forward passes. For computer vision, BinaryConnect [ 8 ] demonstrated that { − 1 , + 1 } \{-1,+1\} weights suffice for image classification on CIFAR-10. XNOR-Net [ 9 ] extended this to ImageNet-scale classification by binarizing both weights and activations. However, these approaches relied on convolutional architectures and did not address sequential modeling challenges. II-C 1-Bit Language Models Recent work has begun exploring extreme quantization for transformers. BitNet [ 10 ] introduced learnable scaling factors for 1-bit transformer training, demonstrating that { − 1 , + 1 } \{-1,+1\} binary weights could achieve competitive perplexity on moderate-scale language modeling. BitNet b1.58 [ 11 ] extended this to ternary { − 1 , 0 , + 1 } \{-1,0,+1\} quantization with 1.58-bit effective precision, training models up to 70B parameters on trillions of tokens. These works demonstrate the possibility of 1-bit language modeling at scale but leave several questions unanswered: Can 1-bit models succeed under resource constraints (single GPU, moderate data)? Do quantized representations transfer effectively to downstream tasks? What layer-wise patterns characterize successful quantization? II-D Efficient Small Language Models Complementary to quantization, research on small language models explores whether compact architectures can acquire meaningful linguistic capabilities. TinyStories [ 12 ] demonstrated that models under 50M parameters trained on synthetic children’s stories exhibit coherent narrative generation, providing a controlled testbed for studying language acquisition. TinyLLaMA [ 13 ] scaled this to 1.1B parameters with optimized training recipes, while Phi-1.5 [ 14 ] emphasized data quality over quantity with carefully curated training corpora. Our work combines insights from both quantization and efficient model design, applying native 1-bit training to the small model regime. Unlike BitNet b1.58 which targets billion-scale models with massive compute, we focus on resource-constrained training (single T4 GPU). Table III compares TernaryLM against a spectrum of full-precision baselines and smaller architectural variants. Our 1-bit model achieves a validation perplexity (PPL) of 58.42, placing it in a competitive mid-range between high-capacity models and ultra-compact baselines. Specifically, TernaryLM stands only 7.19 points (13.8% relative) above the equivalent full-precision 132M architecture, while significantly outperforming smaller full-precision variants like the TinyStories-33M and 1-layer models. Figure 1 shows training dynamics. Loss decreases monotonically from 7.35 to 4.02 over 15 epochs without divergence or oscillation, confirming that our STE-based optimization with RMSNorm achieves stable convergence despite discrete weight constraints. Fig. 1 : Training loss convergence for TernaryLM across three different datasets (TinyStories, WritingPrompts and Shakespeare), demonstrating stable optimization under 1-bit ternary quantization. IV-B Training Stability Across Datasets To verify that stable optimization is not specific to the low-entropy TinyStories corpus, we train TernaryLM on two additional datasets with distinct linguistic characteristics: WritingPrompts [ 18 ] , a dataset of longer creative narratives with higher lexical and structural diversity and and Shakespeare, a classical literary corpus featuring archaic vocabulary and poetic structure. Figure 1 shows that all three training runs exhibit smooth, monotonic loss decrease. While WritingPrompts and Shakespeare converge more slowly than TinyStories—reflecting their higher entropy and linguistic complexity—optimization remains numerically stable throughout all 15 epochs. Shakespeare, despite its unique linguistic properties including verse structure and early modern English syntax, demonstrates comparable stability to modern prose datasets. The consistent convergence patterns across these diverse corpora—ranging from simple children’s stories to creative fiction to classical literature—suggest our training protocol generalizes robustly across varied data distributions and linguistic domains. This multi-dataset validation strengthens the evidence that 1-bit quantization with our proposed architecture maintains stable gradient flow regardless of corpus characteristics. IV-C Downstream Fine-tuning We evaluate downstream transfer by fine-tuning on GLUE benchmark tasks [ 19 ] . For all experiments, we freeze the quantized backbone and train only a task-specific classifier head (768-dim hidden layer with Tanh activation). TABLE IV : Fine-tuning results on GLUE benchmark tasks. Model MRPC F1 SST-2 Acc CoLA MCC Avg BERT-Base 84.98 92.43 56.78 78.06 DistilBERT 82.31 91.12 51.32 74.92 TinyBERT 80.45 89.67 48.91 73.01 TernaryLM 82.47 88.92 47.23 72.87 MRPC (Paraphrase Detection): TernaryLM achieves 82.47% F1 score, only 2.51 points below BERT-Base (84.98%). This demonstrates that 1-bit quantized representations preserve the semantic similarity information required for paraphrase identification. SST-2 (Sentiment Analysis): We observe 88.92% accuracy, a 3.51 point gap from BERT-Base. Binary sentiment classification proves relatively robust to quantization. CoLA (Linguistic Acceptability): The largest gap appears on CoLA (47.23% vs 56.78% MCC), suggesting that fine-grained grammaticality judgments are more sensitive to quantization noise. This aligns with the intuition that subtle syntactic features require higher precision representations. Overall, TernaryLM achieves competitive performance with efficient model variants (DistilBERT, TinyBERT) while using dramatically lower precision, validating that quantized pre-training produces useful representations for downstream tasks. Key findings: Memory: TernaryLM requires 498MB inference memory versus 1,197MB for full-precision BERT-Base—a 2.4 × 	imes reduction. This enables deployment on memory-constrained devices where full-precision models are infeasible. Latency: Per-token latency is 9.41ms for TernaryLM versus 9.52ms for BERT-Base, achieving near-parity. The minor speedup reflects that our implementation uses the same matrix multiply kernels; specialized ternary kernels could yield further improvements. Storage: Model weight storage drops from 438MB (FP32) to 132MB (ternary), a 3.3 × 	imes reduction enabling efficient model distribution and on-device caching. Practical impact: These efficiency gains translate directly to deployment capabilities. A device with 1GB GPU memory that cannot host BERT-Base can comfortably run TernaryLM with headroom for batching. Multi-model serving scenarios benefit from reduced per-model footprint. V Quantization Analysis V-A Layer-wise Sparsity Patterns To understand how quantization affects different network components, we analyze per-layer sparsity—the fraction of weights quantized to zero. Figure 3 visualizes these patterns. Fig. 3 : Per-layer sparsity scores across transformer depth. Middle layers (L5-L9) exhibit highest quantization friendliness with 60-62% sparsity, while early/late layers show moderate 45-55% sparsity. Key findings: • Middle layers (L5-L9) achieve highest sparsity scores (60-62%), indicating strong compatibility with extreme quantization. These layers primarily encode abstract semantic features that tolerate discrete representation. • Early layers (L1-L4) show moderate sparsity (48-55%), reflecting their role in token-level and syntactic processing where fine-grained distinctions matter more. • Late layers (L10-L12) exhibit similar moderate patterns (45-52%), potentially because output-adjacent representations require higher precision for accurate next-token prediction. • Embedding layer shows lowest effective sparsity (35%), motivating our decision to keep it in full precision. These patterns suggest that non-uniform quantization —applying higher precision to sensitive layers—could improve quality while preserving most efficiency gains. V-B Weight Distribution Evolution Fig. 4 : Evolution of weight distributions during training at epochs 1, 5, 10, and 15, showing convergence toward ternary clustering. Figure 4 shows how weight distributions evolve during training. Initially, weights follow standard initialization (near-Gaussian). As training progresses, the distribution develops three distinct modes corresponding to { − 1 , 0 , + 1 } \{-1,0,+1\} quantization targets. By epoch 15, weights cluster tightly around these ternary values with minimal intermediate values. This organic clustering—rather than forced quantization—indicates that the network genuinely adapts its representations to the discrete constraint, supporting the viability of native 1-bit training. Adaptive scaling is crucial for accommodating layer-wise activation magnitude differences. RMSNorm: Switching to LayerNorm increases PPL by 5.43 points. RMSNorm’s simpler normalization (no mean subtraction) provides more stable gradients for discrete weights. Label smoothing: Mild degradation (2.81 points) without smoothing, which helps prevent overconfident predictions that amplify quantization error. Binary vs ternary: Restricting to { − 1 , + 1 } \{-1,+1\} (no zeros) severely degrades quality (72.18 PPL). The zero value provides essential representational flexibility. Quantized embeddings: The most severe degradation (89.54 PPL) confirms that vocabulary semantics require full precision to avoid token collapse. V-D Qualitative Generation Examples We qualitatively evaluate TernaryLM using nucleus sampling ( p = 0.9 p=0.9 , temperature = 0.8 =0.8 ) across datasets of increasing linguistic complexity. TinyStories “Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She liked to play in the garden with her dog Max. One day, Lily found a beautiful flower. She picked it and showed it to her mom. Her mom smiled and said it was very pretty.” WritingPrompts “She never imagined that today would change her life. There was the first time to be heard the only one. We had to take the day of the sun through the front door.” Shakespeare “O Romeo, Romeo! Why the duke commands, and yet I would— What! The king, ’tis so decreed. My lord, I pray thee, stake my life; For what in thee I know, I must.” TernaryLM generates coherent narratives on low-entropy data and retains stylistic and syntactic cues under higher linguistic complexity, indicating that native 1-bit quantization preserves essential generative structure. VI Conclusion We introduced TernaryLM, a 132M-parameter transformer trained natively with 1-bit ternary quantization that challenges conventional assumptions about minimum precision requirements for language modeling. Our experiments demonstrate that discrete { − 1 , 0 , + 1 } \{-1,0,+1\} weights can achieve validation perplexity competitive with full-precision baselines (58.42 vs 51.23), transfer effectively to downstream tasks (82.47% F1 on MRPC), and deliver substantial efficiency gains (2.4 × 	imes memory reduction with latency parity). Layer-wise analysis reveals non-uniform quantization sensitivity across transformer depth, with middle layers most amenable to extreme compression. These insights motivate future work on mixed-precision architectures that preserve quality in sensitive layers while maximizing compression elsewhere. Limitations: Our study focuses on a controlled setting (TinyStories, 132M parameters). Scaling to larger models and more complex datasets may reveal additional challenges. Our implementation uses standard CUDA kernels; specialized ternary matrix multiply could yield further speedups. Future directions: (1) Scaling 1-bit training to billion-parameter models with efficient distributed training; (2) Developing hardware-optimized ternary kernels for practical deployment speedup; (3) Exploring non-uniform precision allocation based on layer-wise sensitivity; (4) Applying 1-bit quantization to other modalities (vision, speech) and multimodal models. Our results establish native 1-bit quantization as a viable paradigm for efficient neural language models, opening pathways toward practical deployment on resource-constrained devices without sacrificing language understanding capability.
